title: Observability Lite: minimal metric & trace envelope + query budgeting playbook
content:
Purpose:

This is a lightweight, pragmatic observability playbook intended for fast rollout into new inference services and model routes. Goal: get to 90-95% of incident detection and most common perf investigations with 20% of the metric/trace surface area we currently maintain.

Why 'Lite' (context):
- Full telemetry surfaces are expensive: query costs, dashboard maintenance, and alert fatigue.
- Many services share common failure modes (cold starts, KV-cache misses, batching impact, model fallback). A minimal, well-designed set of signals + a standard trace envelope covers the majority of investigations.
- This doc proposes the minimal metric set, a canonical trace context/envelope, dashboard tile templates with approximate query cost per refresh, and an incremental migration plan.

Scope:
- Applies to inference routes (hosted API + Dedicated pools) and internal platform components (router, batcher, kv-cache layer).
- Not a full replacement for SRE-grade SLOs; this is for quick-onboarding services and dev teams that need practical observability without heavy instrumentation.

Minimal Metric Set (intent: high signal-to-noise, cheap to compute):
1) request.count (per-route) - COUNTER - tags: route, model, region, customer_tier  -- primary traffic signal
2) request.latency.p50/p95/p99 (per-route) - HISTOGRAM-derived quantiles - tags as above -- latency slices, downstream impact
3) tokens.generated.per_request.mean - GAUGE (derived) - tags: route, model - useful for cost correlation
4) kvcache.hit_rate (per-model/pool) - GAUGE - tags: model, pool - key to batching effectiveness
5) batch.size.p50/p95 - HISTOGRAM-derived - tags: pool, route - helps correlate throughput vs latency
6) gpu.utilization.percent (per-host/pool) - GAUGE - hardware saturation
7) model.fallback.count (per-route) - COUNTER - indicates graceful degradation
8) error.count.by_code (per-route) - COUNTER - 4xx/5xx/timeout/hw-failure - basic health
9) synthetic.ping.latency (probe for route) - GAUGE - cheap synthetic canary
10) sampling.trace.proportion (per-service) - GAUGE - indicates tracing rate for the service

Notes on aggregation and cardinality:
- Primary aggregation keys: route, model, pool, region. Avoid adding customer_id or session_id as default tag (fanout risk).
- Use coarse model tags for model family + size (e.g., star-llama-13b/q4) not full commit sha.
- Bucket latency histograms aligned to common slices: [<5ms, 5-20ms, 20-100ms, 100-500ms, >500ms] to simplify dashboards.

Canonical Trace Context / Envelope (text description of recommended trace fields to propagate):
- trace_id (UUID/v4) - root identifier
- span_id (hex) - current span
- parent_span_id - optional
- service.name - e.g., router, batcher, kv-cache, runtime
- service.instance_id - host|container id for fast lookup
- route - logical route name (not full URL)
- model.version - coarse version tag (e.g., v2.1 canary)
- request.id - request-level id (matches request.count / logs)
- tokens.so_far - integer (useful for multi-chunk streaming traces)
- kv_cache.hit - boolean (true/false) or kv_cache.delta_ms - time spent in cache
- batch.size - integer
- fallback_reason - short enum if fallback triggered
- sampling.priority - integer (trace sampler decision)

Propagation and context rules:
- Ensure the envelope travels on both sync HTTP/gRPC paths and internal message bus headers.
- For batched requests, record a 'batch' span that contains child spans for per-item processing (lightweight stub spans are fine).
- Keep trace span payload under 2KB (no full prompt copies). If you need prompt text, store a redacted hash/ID and write full text only to a short-term index with strict access control.

Dashboard Tile Templates + Estimated Query Cost (ballpark):
- Assumptions: metrics stored in TSDB with per-query cost roughly correlated to cardinality/time-range. Costs listed are relative: LOW / MED / HIGH. Refresh cadence suggestions included.

1) Service Overview row (one row per route): request.count (last 5m), p95 latency, error.rate, kvcache.hit_rate.
   - Query cost: LOW (simple aggregates over small tag set).
   - Refresh: 30s
   - Good for paging/incident initial triage.

2) Latency heatmap (time vs latency bucket) for high-traffic routes.
   - Query cost: MED (histogram expansion).
   - Refresh: 60s
   - Use only for top N routes (e.g., top 10 by TPS) to limit cost.

3) Batch size distribution and correlation panel (batch.size vs p95 latency).
   - Query cost: MED-HIGH (histogram + join).
   - Refresh: 60-120s.

4) KV-cache diagnostic (hit_rate over time + top keys miss rates).
   - Query cost: MED (if per-key topk used, may spike).
   - Refresh: 120s for topk, 30s for overall hit_rate.

5) Fallback waterfall (count by fallback_reason and correlated latency).
   - Query cost: LOW-MED
   - Refresh: 60s

6) Synthetic canary dashboard (end-to-end latency + trace links for failing synthetics).
   - Query cost: LOW
   - Refresh: 15-30s

Cost control recommendations:
- Limit cardinality on dashboards: add an allowlist for route/model combos.
- Use dashboard templating variables but default to a single selection (e.g., the team or the route owner).
- For heavy-weight panels (histograms, topk), limit time window (last 1h) by default and provide a manual expansion option.
- Precompute or materialize common joins (e.g., batch.size -> latency bucket) as derived metrics where possible.

Tracing sampling and retention guidance:
- Default sample_rate: 1% across all requests for retention cost control.
- Adaptive sampling policy: ramp to 100% for requests that hit error.count>0, or for requests longer than p95 latency threshold.
- Retain full traces for 7 days; keep trace index/metadata for 30 days. Archive anonymized trace indexes for 6 months if needed for audits.
- Use head-based sampling with tail-rerouting for rare error classes (capture all traces that later produce alerts).

Migration plan (incremental rollout to a new route):
1) Implement minimal metrics (request.count, latency quantiles, error.count) + emit request.id. Smoke test in staging. (1 week)
2) Add kvcache metrics + batch.size. Deploy to canary pool (10% traffic). Monitor dashboard cost. (1 week)
3) Add trace envelope and sampling config (start 0.5% sample). Instrument batch span. (3 days)
4) Observe for 2 weeks, collect feedback, and enable adaptive sampling rules for latencies/errors. (2 weeks)
5) Onboard route owner to the lite dashboard; measure query budget usage and prune as needed.

Open questions / unresolved decisions:
- Do we allow optional inclusion of customer_id for enterprise routes? (privacy & cardinality tradeoff)
- Metric naming: use dotted vs snake_case? Current telemetry uses mixed naming; propose standardization in a follow-up RFC.
- Where to store full prompt redactions / hashes for debugging? Propose short-lived index with strict ACLs; need security sign-off (see OBS-721).

Action items (owners):
- Asha: draft RFC for metric naming and derived metrics (due 2024-04-05).
- Miles: prototype dashboard templates and measure query costs on staging (due 2024-03-15).
- Ravi: implement trace envelope headers in router and batcher services (pr: infra#829).
- Evelyn: coordinate privacy review for prompt-hash storage (linked ticket OBS-721).

Quick reference (copyable snippet for infra teams):
- Minimal metric tags: {route, model_family, pool, region}
- Trace header names: X-Trace-Id, X-Span-Id, X-Service-Name, X-Route, X-Model-Version, X-Request-Id
- Recommended default sampling: 0.01 (1%) with adaptive escalation for errors/latency spikes

Notes and rough history:
- Derived from debugging sessions in Jan-Feb 2024 where we found 70% of incidents were resolved with the service overview + 1 trace.
- This is deliberately conservative: aim for low-cost telemetry that still provides good investigative power.

If you want to iterate: add concrete PromQL / Datadog query examples and I'll drop them in next revision.

End of doc.
